To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the ingestion of feed and the gastric administration of feed ingredients, including a mixture of indispensable (essential) amino acids, caused a positive secretory release of prolactin in stallions.
the ingestion of feed and gastric administration of feed ingredients resulted in increases in plasma concentrations of prolactine, glucose, insulin and total amino acids.

the ingestion of feed and the gastric administration of feed constituents (corn starch, egg albumin) increased plasma concentrations of glucose, insulin, total amino acids, and prolactin in the stallion.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of feed on the secretion of hormones.

the development of a method for the preparation of a series of 3,5-dinitrobenzoyl amino acids and the use of the 3,5-DNB amino acids in a method for determining the amino acid composition of proteins.
the study of the effect of the ingestion of feed or the gastric administration of water and feed components on plasma concentrations of prolactine and some other metabolic parameters in the horse.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the results obtained in this study are in agreement with the hypothesis that the presence of feed in the stomach is the primary stimulus to release of prolactin and that this release is a result of the presence of amino acids in the stomach.

feeding of a complete feed mixture results in an increase in plasma concentrations of prolactine, glucose, insulin and total amino acids, whereas administration of water, salt, egg albumin or corn starch results in a significant increase in glucose, insulin and amino acids.
the results of this study are consistent with previous studies that have shown that feeding of feed or feed components can result in an increase in plasma prolactin concentration in horses.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the feeding of a meal stimulates the release of a number of hormones, including insulin, prolactin, and total amino acid concentrations.

the feeding of pelleted feed or the gastric administration of water or a mixture of amino acids or a hydrolyzed caseinate resulted in increased plasma concentrations of glucose, insulin, total amino acids and urea nitrogen, while prolactin concentrations decreased.
we have found that prolactin is secreted after feeding and that the secretion is related to the amount of amino acids absorbed.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the plasma concentrations of prolactins, glucose, insulin and urea nitrogen, as well as total amino acids in horses are influenced by feed and feed components, and these changes occur at different times.
there is a positive correlation between the concentration of amino acids and insulin in the blood.
the plasma concentrations of prolactins, glucose, insulin and total amino acids are affected by the feed and its components.
